name: Helix Corp Cubicle Compliance Day Set
description: The uniform of invisible labor. A mid-weight synth-wool blend blazer in Helix Corp mandated slate-grey, cut boxy enough to fit nearly any body type off the rack — which is exactly the point. The lapels are narrow and slightly shiny from dry-cleaning friction, and a small embossed Helix Corp service tag is heat-pressed inside the collar. Underneath, a white broadcloth dress shirt with a subtle grid weave, the collar slightly stiff from industrial starch, two buttons always threatening to gap at the chest. Trousers are straight-cut in matching slate-grey synth-wool, with a barely-perceptible shine at the knees from desk chair contact. A single pleat runs down each leg, machine-pressed each Monday. Black faux-leather belt, no buckle ornamentation. The shoes are Helix-issued matte black cap-toe oxfords, cushioned enough for transit but not for comfort — the kind of shoe that always looks slightly too big. A lanyard with a Helix Corp RFID badge clip hangs at the chest, the badge itself scratched from years of swipe-gate use. Hair and accessories must conform to the Helix Corp Appearance Code (HAC-7), which means nothing unusual, nothing memorable.
functionality: Badge-clip lanyard integration, RFID-passthrough collar tag for building access, stain-resistant trouser finish, machine-washable shirt, standard aug-port clearance at collar back for basic neural ports only
what_it_says: You are employed. You are compliant. You have not yet been promoted and you are not trying to look like you have. The outfit says nothing personal about the wearer because that is the point — individuality is a liability at this tier. The slight wear patterns tell colleagues exactly how long you've been here and how little has changed.
worn_by: anyone on their first year at a corponation desk job
price_range: Φ180–Φ240 (often deducted from first paycheck as 'uniform acquisition fee')
story_hooks: A character wearing this exact uniform is mistaken for a Helix Corp insider by a street contact — the badge clone on the lanyard is the only thing standing between them and a secure floor they have no business being on.
The HAC-7 dress code is used as evidence in a wrongful termination case — a worker was fired for wearing a non-regulation belt buckle, and the outfit becomes exhibit A in a labor tribunal.

Someone has been wearing this uniform for eleven years. The shine at the knees is a timestamp. A new colleague notices and asks how long they've been waiting for a promotion — the silence that follows says everything.
related_entities: TESSERA CORPONATION Aegis CorpSec Hardened Security BCI

physical_description.visual_profile: A uniform of corporate anonymity — boxy, deliberately unremarkable silhouette designed to obscure rather than flatter. The overall impression is one of institutional conformity: the blazer hangs slightly loose, the shirt sits beneath it in sterile white, and the trousers are cut to standardize rather than individualize. This is clothing engineered to be forgotten.
physical_description.fit: Intentionally oversized and relaxed through the torso and shoulders to accommodate varied body types straight off the rack. The trousers are straight-cut with minimal taper, and the blazer's boxy cut ensures no definition at the waist. The shirt collar sits slightly stiff and formal. Nothing is tailored; everything is mass-produced for interchangeability.
physical_description.primary_material: Mid-weight synth-wool blend for the blazer and trousers; white broadcloth with subtle grid weave for the shirt. All treated for durability and institutional cleaning cycles. Faux-leather belt and matte black cap-toe oxford shoes complete the ensemble.
physical_description.texture: The blazer's fabric shows a subtle sheen from repeated dry-cleaning friction on the lapels. The shirt collar is stiff from industrial starch application. The trousers display a barely-perceptible shine at the knees from prolonged desk-chair contact. The shoes are matte and utilitarian. Overall: smooth, sterile, and worn into blandness.
physical_description.color_scheme: Mandated slate-grey (blazer and trousers), bright institutional white (shirt), matte black (belt and shoes). No pattern beyond the subtle grid weave in the broadcloth. No accents. The color palette itself enforces conformity.
physical_description.closures: Standard two-button blazer closure; two-button shirt front with stiff collar. Straight-zip fly trousers with black faux-leather belt (no buckle). Cap-toe oxfords with basic lacing. All closures are functional and anonymous.
distinctive_features: Embossed Helix Corp service tag heat-pressed inside collar
Lanyard with RFID badge clip at chest — the badge itself visibly scratched from years of swipe-gate use
Machine-pressed single pleat down each trouser leg, reset every Monday
Barely-perceptible knee shine from desk chair wear
Industrial starch stiffness in shirt collar
No ornamentation, no variation, no personality
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2 corporate — the uniform of salaried desk workers in megacorp hierarchy. Expensive enough to signal employment stability, bland enough to signal obedience.
physical_description.cultural_context: The wearer is a Helix Corp employee, likely in middle-tier administrative or technical role. This outfit broadcasts institutional loyalty, regulatory compliance, and acceptance of the corporate appearance code. It signals someone who has chosen (or been forced into) invisible labor within the system. Hair and all accessories conform to HAC-7 standards — nothing memorable, nothing individual.
physical_description.condition_typical: Pristine in the moment of morning dressing, but subtly worn by afternoon. The knees show desk-chair contact patterns. The lapels carry the faint sheen of institutional dry-cleaning. The RFID badge is visibly scratched and worn from daily gate-swipe rituals. The shirt collar begins to lose its starch by mid-day. Everything is maintained just well enough to pass inspection, but nothing shows pride of ownership.
